tr.td: September to October 1996, with court proceedings from 1999 to 2008
TNT Limited, an Australian transport group, bid for by the Dutch company KPN
One count of insider trading and two counts of structuring cash transactions to avoid reporting
Convicted in 1999, conviction quashed in 2000, convicted again in 2002; appeal dismissed in 2006
Simon Gautier Hannes, an executive director of Macquarie Corporate Finance, part of Macquarie Bank
TNT call options with a strike price of $2, maturing in November 1996
About $2 million, according to ASIC and the Court of Criminal Appeal
The Australian Securities Commission (later ASIC), the Australian Federal Police and the surveillance division of the Australian Stock Exchange
17 September 1999: two years and two months, plus fines of $110,000, with release after 18 months
13 December 2002: two years and six months, with the time already served counted
New South Wales Court of Criminal Appeal, 24 November 2006; High Court special leave refused in March 2008, then re-argument listed for 13 June 2008

li.a: Australian Securities and Investments Commission: media release 99/329, "Simon Gautier Hannes receives gaol sentence", 17 September 1999
ABC, The World Today: "Former Macquarie executive jailed again", 13 December 2002
The Age: "Insider trading sentence extended", 13 December 2002
Sydney Morning Herald: "Hannes given rare second chance", 12 May 2008
NSW Court of Criminal Appeal: R v Hannes [2000] NSWCCA 503, 1 December 2000 (archived copy of the AustLII text)
NSW Court of Criminal Appeal: Hannes v DPP (Cth) (No 2) [2006] NSWCCA 373, 24 November 2006 (archived copy of the AustLII text)

content.p: In September 1996 a man calling himself Mark Booth opened a share-trading account in Sydney with a small pile of bank cheques and bought call options on TNT Limited, a transport company. Two weeks later a Dutch company announced a takeover of TNT and the options were worth about $2 million. The name was an alias. Two juries convicted Simon Hannes, a senior Macquarie Bank dealmaker, of insider trading and of two offences of structuring cash transactions to avoid the reporting rules, in a case that an ABC reporter and The Age described as Australia's biggest for insider trading.

Hannes was convicted in 1999, won an appeal in 2000, was tried and convicted again in 2002, and lost a second appeal in 2006. He served prison time twice. He did not keep the profit: the corporate regulator froze the money within days. His case became a rare example of a prosecution for insider trading inside Australia's close-knit corporate world, and it ended up in the High Court in 2008 over a claim that one of the judges had once advised him.

Hannes had held senior positions at Macquarie Bank or its corporate finance arm since the mid-1980s. The Court of Criminal Appeal's 2006 judgment, summarising trial evidence, described him as one of about a dozen executive directors of Macquarie Corporate Finance. Macquarie's managing director told the second trial that Hannes had headed the executives advising one party to the CRA and RTZ merger, at that point the largest merger Australia had seen, and that his grasp of takeover work was outstanding.

In 1996 the same division was advising TNT. According to the 2006 judgment, a meeting in Hong Kong in May 1996 discussed a possible deal between TNT and the Dutch post office company KPN, most likely a friendly takeover of TNT. The advisory work went by code names, first "Project Mercury" and then "Project Tennis", and its team worked on a secured floor of the bank. A reporter for ABC radio, discussing the case in 2002, gave the project's name as "Project Hannes"; the court record names it Project Tennis.

Hannes was not on that team. The court heard, though, that he had a desk on the same floor, next to a team member's, and that he could reach the team's electronic records from his computer terminal. Bank rules forbade executives to trade in the securities of any client the bank was advising; Macquarie kept an "embargo list" of such companies, and TNT was on it for the whole period.

Hannes took leave in mid-1996, returned to work on 1 July and went on indefinite leave from 1 August, but he kept his desk, computer and keys. The court was told he asked a team member in July what value he had reached for TNT and challenged whether it was too high, that he attended a bank dinner on 22 July where a document mentioned Project Tennis, and that he went to a conference on 25 to 27 July at which a slide mentioned the project and a possible fee of $5 million to $10 million. A document called "Tennis Next Steps", prepared on 27 or 28 August, recorded that KPN was prepared to pay up to $2.40 a share and that TNT would accept $2.50. It would have been available on his terminal. Security records also showed him entering the secure floor after hours on several dates in July, and again on 21 August and on 8 and 15 September.
The prosecution case, as set out in both appeal judgments, was that over a few days in September 1996 Hannes built a false trading identity. Its steps were these.

On 5 September a man giving the name Mark Booth rented a mailbox at a Mail Boxes Etc shop in Mosman and paid in cash. Around that time, the 2006 judgment records, Hannes faxed a firm called Leveraged Equities asking for $200,000 to be moved into his own account at the Commonwealth Bank in Wynyard. (The 2000 judgment instead says the transfer came from an account he controlled at the brokers Ord Minnett.)

On 6 September three cash withdrawals were made from that account, of $20,000, $10,000 and $10,000. At the Pitt Street and Martin Place branch a bank officer made him sign a Significant Cash Transaction Report form headed "$10,000 or more". The other two withdrawals were reported electronically to Austrac, the agency that administers the cash reporting law. The Crown's case was that this was the moment Hannes learned of the reporting obligation.

On 9 September the withdrawals changed shape. At six branches across Sydney he drew out one sum of $9,900, four of $9,000 and one of $6,000, all under the $10,000 threshold. The same day a man calling himself M. Booth bought nine bank cheques for cash from nine different branches of four banks: eight of $9,000 and one of $9,900. Each was made out to the Ord Minnett Cash Management Trust, and the cheques went into an account opened in the name M. Booth, with a first cheque of $9,000 having been bought on 6 September. By the 2006 judgment's count the account held $90,900. The account application gave a Mosman mailbox as its address and the Intercontinental Hotel as a contact; the Crown proved that nobody of that name had been resident at the hotel.

Hannes's prosecutors read the splitting as deliberate. Chief Justice Spigelman wrote in 2000 that the pattern, small sums at many branches in different parts of the city, was capable of being seen as an effort to make the transactions hard to link and to ensure no bank officer remembered the customer. One detail he picked out: the same "M. Booth" bought two cheques of the same amount, payable to the same account, at two different banks in Roseville on one day.

On 17 September "Booth" telephoned the Ord Minnett stockbroker Andrew Staehli, asked to trade options and wanted a price on TNT November $2 call options. Staehli quoted between one and two cents, called it a fairly risky option to buy, and was asked to invest the roughly $90,000 sitting in the account. "Booth" asked for the application forms to be left at reception. They came back completed in capitals, with a typed letter of instructions signed "M Booth", and a sponsorship form witnessed by a man named "Alexi Voltraint" of "52 Railway Road, Petersham". There is no Railway Road in Petersham, and the occupant of 52 Railway Street had never heard of him.

TNT shares were then trading at about $1.56 to $1.59. Between 18 and 20 September the broker bought what was later described as 5,000 option contracts. On 19 September "Booth" paid cash for a voicemail answering service in Surry Hills. When told on 20 September that $1,500 of the deposit was left unspent, he was, the court heard, annoyed.

At 9 a.m. on 2 October 1996 the Australian Stock Exchange announced a takeover bid for TNT by KPN at $2.45 a share. TNT's shares rose to $2.25 and the options soared. "Booth" wrote to Staehli on 3 October asking him to hold the options until 4 November and then sell. A letter the next day, which the court heard was also signed "M. Booth", complained that the publicity about suspected insider trading was "extremely disturbing, as even airing of such allegations would be professionally damaging to me." It enclosed a statement that said he had had no knowledge of a takeover bid. A later letter instructed Ord Minnett to pay out the money as the regulator recommended, because he wished the investors from whom he bought the options "not to suffer loss". The sale of the options brought in $2,039,710, which was credited to the account between 25 and 28 November.
content.h2: Finding the man behind the name
content.p: The regulator moved fast. ASIC's 1999 release said its investigation of "Mark Booth's" trading began within 24 hours of the 2 October announcement, and that within two days it had obtained court orders freezing the roughly $2 million profit. The 2006 judgment dates the Federal Court restraint to 4 October 1996 and notes that "Mark Booth", named as defendant, never appeared. ASIC said the money was ultimately returned to the people who had sold the options. The inquiry was run jointly with the Federal Police and with the exchange's own surveillance division, and ASIC credited what it called sophisticated investigation techniques with identifying Hannes as the buyer.

The evidence the courts described was largely paper and handwriting. Hannes left Australia on 14 November 1996 and returned on 17 December. On 17 January 1997 federal police searched his home and seized his computer, from which records that had been deleted but not wiped were later recovered. They contained wording close to passages in the "Booth" letters, a fragment of a letter about mailbox rent, and the repeated name M Booth with the Mosman mailbox address. A notebook carried indentations that a technique called ESDA turned back into text, including a column of "M Booth" signatures and a page headed "Should I visit ASC or not" that argued the author's innocence and treated the author and "Mark" as different people. His 1996 diary had a handwritten entry for the evening of 16 October in which a street number had been changed from 50 to 51. The court noted that a book-club member lived at 51 Railway Street in Petersham, and that Hannes belonged to the club and had visited her house.

Bank tellers and others gave identification evidence from a board of photographs, and handwriting opinion evidence was given on the application forms. A security camera at the Leichhardt branch of the National Australia Bank had photographed the buyer of one cheque. Shown the picture by police, Hannes said: "That could be me." He also said: "It's probably me, because it looks a bit like me, doesn't it?"
content.h2: The defence: a partner nobody could find
content.p: Hannes was interviewed by federal agents on 17 January 1997, and the record of the interview went before both juries. He opened by saying he was innocent of insider trading. He said he had agreed to form an investment syndicate with an English friend whom he would only call Mr X, that he was to put in up to $100,000 with any profits meant for his sister Mignon, whose married name is Booth, and that Mr X would do the investing. Asked for $100,000 in cash and then for cheques, he said, he had simply done as asked. He said Mr X later told him he had bought TNT options, which upset him because TNT was a Macquarie client and the investment breached the rules. He said he had never discussed the bank's TNT work with Mr X.

The prosecution answered that account on several fronts. The Court of Criminal Appeal noted that he said a Roseville teller told him no Sydney bank could supply $100,000 in cash and that a Wynyard employee advised him to visit a series of branches. The Crown called staff from both branches, none of whom recalled such a request, and Wynyard staff said they would not have suggested visiting several branches. The court also noted that, asked why he had not obtained a single cheque, he said he did not know. Spigelman CJ held in 2000 that the jury could treat parts of his interview as admissions that he had obtained all nine cheques in the name Booth. Hannes did not give evidence at his first trial.

The first trial in the New South Wales District Court was, in the Court of Criminal Appeal's words, long and complex: 36 sitting days before the summing-up, 45 Crown witnesses including three experts, two defence witnesses, and more than 200 exhibits. The ABC's reporter, who covered it, said two earlier trials had been aborted. The jury returned guilty verdicts on the two cash-structuring counts on 6 August 1999 on the eighth day of deliberation, and on the insider trading count on 11 August after being unable at first to agree.

On 17 September 1999 Judge Cecily Backhouse sentenced him to four years for insider trading, adjusted to two years and two months because New South Wales had no remission, plus four months for each of the two structuring counts, to run concurrently. She fined him $100,000 on the insider trading count and $5,000 on each of the other two, and set release after 18 months on recognisance. ASIC announced that Hannes had appealed. The prosecutors in turn appealed the sentence as too lenient. The ABC reporter later recalled the fine as $200,000, which does not match ASIC's figures.

Hannes served almost 16 months, according to the Sydney Morning Herald (the ABC and The Age put it at 15), before the Court of Criminal Appeal decided his appeal on 1 December 2000. Chief Justice Spigelman and Justices Studdert and Dowd quashed all three convictions and ordered a new trial. The decision turned on the "Weissensteiner" direction the trial judge had given the jury, which allows a jury to draw inferences more readily against an accused who does not give evidence; a High Court decision issued after the trial, RPS v The Queen, had narrowed when that was permitted. The court also held that telling the jury it was irrelevant whether "another person was involved" risked confusing them.

The Chief Justice nevertheless called the Crown case a strong one, and rejected the argument that the jury's long deliberations showed otherwise; he read them as a sign that this jury had carefully reviewed the evidence. He wrote that the decision to retry was best left to the prosecution given the short extra penalty a further conviction would probably bring, and he said the delay in hearing the appeal was almost entirely the appellant's own, partly from waiting for counsel of his choice. The Crown's appeal against the sentence was dismissed.
content.h2: Second trial and the sentence of 2002
content.p: A jury in the New South Wales Supreme Court convicted Hannes a second time in 2002. On 13 December Justice Bruce James sentenced him to two years and six months. As The Age reported it, the judge reinstated the original two years and two months for the insider trading charge, added four months for the two counts under the Financial Transactions Reports Act, and re-imposed the $100,000 fine. With about 15 months already served, the ABC reported he would need to serve only four more months, with release possible in April 2003.

The judge's remarks were reported two ways. The Age said he found Hannes had poor prospects of rehabilitation, had shown no contrition, and fell in the worst category for this type of white collar offence, even though the regulator's quick action meant Hannes never received the $2 million profit. The ABC's reporter, in court, recalled that the judge also called him once a brilliant merchant banker, took his previous good character into account, and noted that Hannes had not benefited and no one had lost money. She said he showed no reaction, and the judge observed that the publicity had ruined his life. The sentencing hearing ended with the judge adjourning for a stay application.

The trial also heard good words from colleagues. A Macquarie assistant director who sat at the next desk told the jury his reputation was excellent for ability and integrity. The Court of Criminal Appeal later said it was appropriate for the judge to warn the jury against drawing an adverse inference from the defence not calling or questioning other witnesses on character.

Hannes appealed the second conviction, representing himself over eight hearing days in November 2005. The three-judge panel of Justice Basten, Justice Barr and Justice Hall delivered its decision on 24 November 2006, dismissing the conviction appeal and refusing leave to appeal the sentence, which he had by then served in full.

His grounds attacked the way the charge was framed, the identification photoboard, character evidence, the handwriting expert, the admission of evidence about the Project Tennis negotiations, and the directions to the jury. Justices Barr and Hall rejected those grounds. The court held that the photoboard, made of images of members of the public caught on bank cameras, was fairly put together and that the jury was properly cautioned about it, and that it was open to the jury to find he had information about planned meetings and who would attend. They also held that it did not matter that parts of the information were public, because the particularised information as a whole was not generally available. The court said it had no reasonable doubt that he took part in the conduct in the insider trading count and that the cash transactions were done for the dominant purpose of avoiding reports.

Justice Basten dissented on the first count. He thought the indictment and the evidence did not fit. The indictment's particulars said there was a prospect of an offer above $2 a share, while the evidence pointed to an offer between $2.40 and $2.50. He thought that uncertainty amounted to a substantial miscarriage of justice and that a verdict of acquittal should replace the conviction. He was outvoted.
content.h2: The High Court and the question about a judge
content.p: Hannes took the case to the High Court. In March 2008 the Chief Justice, Murray Gleeson, and Justice Dyson Heydon refused special leave to appeal. In May 2008 the Sydney Morning Herald reported that Justice Gummow had listed the matter for "re-argument" on 13 June, after Hannes lodged a submission on 1 May. The submission said Justice Heydon should have disclosed at the start of the March hearing that, before his appointment to the bench in 2003, he had advised Hannes on his insider trading defence. A fair-minded lay observer, it argued, could reasonably apprehend bias. It added that the concern might be stronger if the observer learned that the advice may have been followed and some appeal grounds based on it.

The newspaper noted that Justice Heydon had not appeared for Hannes at any trial or appeal; that work had gone to the barristers Lionel Robberds, David Jackson and Ian Barker. Tim Game, a senior counsel, acted for the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions throughout. Hannes represented himself at the hearing the week before, as he had on his second appeal. Reporting from May 2008 ends with the re-argument listed for 13 June.
